title: The serpent who kept the precepts
hook: the naga prince Bhuridatta keeps the uposatha even when captured (Jataka 543)

segments.voice: Yesterday: khanti, patience, and Prince Canda pleading without hatred until true words stopped a sacrifice. Your line: saved by truth. Today, someone who keeps a vow with his life on the line.

A great snake lies coiled on top of an anthill by a river, perfectly still. He isn't hunting, and he isn't asleep. He's keeping a holy day. In the Jataka he is Bhuridatta, a prince of the nagas, the serpent beings of the waters, who has come up into the human world to keep the observance without distraction. He has made a vow about anyone who finds him there. Today, someone does.
screen: `A SNAKE ON AN ANTHILL.` → `KEEPING A HOLY DAY.` → `A VOW ABOUT ANYONE WHO COMES.`

segments.voice: The uposatha is the Buddhist observance day, when lay people take on extra precepts and keep them for the day and night. Bhuridatta's vow, the story says, is that if anyone wants his skin, his flesh, anything at all, they can take it; he won't break his precepts to stop them. Then the betrayal. A hunter who knows where he lies betrays him to a snake charmer, in a bargain over a magic jewel. The charmer seizes him and crushes him into a basket. Bhuridatta has the power to destroy his captor, the story says, with a single angry look. He won't give him even that. He keeps his eyes shut rather than look at the man in anger, so his precept holds. The charmer drags him from village to village and makes him dance for coins, and still he keeps it. At last his family searches for him, finds him, and wins him free. Tradition pairs this tale with sila, virtue. Not a show of goodness for an audience, but a line kept when breaking it would be easy and would even seem fair. The precept isn't tested on a quiet day. It's tested in the basket.
screen: `THE OBSERVANCE DAY AND HIS VOW.` · `BETRAYED TO A SNAKE CHARMER.` · `NOT EVEN AN ANGRY LOOK.` · `HIS FAMILY WINS HIM FREE.` · then, large: `HE KEPT IT.`

segments.voice: Pick a single precept, like not speaking falsely or not taking what isn't given, and picture the moment today when it will be hardest to keep. See yourself in that moment, holding the line quietly, the way the serpent kept his eyes closed.
Uposatha. The observance day Bhuridatta the naga prince was keeping when, captured and mistreated, he wouldn't even look at his captor in anger. Today's word.
Your line: he kept it. No speech, no drama, just the line, held. Day eight hundred forty-three, done.

howItsDone: On uposatha days, tied to the phases of the moon, Buddhist lay people may visit a temple, listen to teaching, and take extra precepts for the day and night, such as eating no food after midday.

notes: Whole story paraphrased; nothing quoted. Word is the index's singular 'precept'; the title is plural. Suggest aligning the index.

Confirm: Bhuridatta lies on an anthill by the Yamuna to keep uposatha; his vow to let anyone take his skin/flesh; the brahmin hunter (Nesada) betrays him to the snake charmer Alambayana for a jewel; he refrains from looking in anger lest his gaze destroy the charmer (script: 'keeps his eyes shut'); he is made to dance in villages; his brothers (Sudassana and others) and sister win him free.
howItsDone's 'no food after midday' is one of the eight uposatha precepts; confirm phrasing.
Confirm the traditional pairing Bhuridatta = sila (virtue).
Editor: cut the stock line 'here's the remarkable detail'.

Audit: 'leads a charmer to him in exchange for a magic jewel' implied the hunter was paid with the jewel; in Jataka 543 the jewel's direction of exchange (Nesada holds the jewel; Alambayana wants it) is easy to get backwards, so the script and match now say only 'a bargain over a magic jewel'. Keeper to confirm the exact deal. Also fixed a doubled 'even'.
